item.title: NASA+ Content Coming to Big Screen at Greenbelt, Maryland Cinema
item.description:
NASA announced Monday that NASA+ content has found its first theatrical home at The Greenbelt Cinema in Greenbelt, Maryland, expanding the agency’s reach across major viewing platforms and bringing space even closer to home.
“The National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 calls us to share our story of space exploration with the broadest possible audience, and our partners help us accomplish that,” said Rebecca Sirmons, general manager of NASA+ at the agency’s Headquarters in Washington. “Artemis II captured the imagination of the Artemis generation, but we are just getting started. With Artemis III on the horizon and our sights set on building humanity’s first Moon Base, this is only the beginning of our story being told, and we’ll continue sharing transparent, engaging content every step of the way.”
NASA and The Greenbelt Cinema will kick off their partnership with screenings of the NASA+ original documentary “The Europa Concept,” which follows NASA’s journey to investigate the science driving future exploration of Europa, Jupiter’s icy moon. Dates for screenings will be announced soon on NASA.gov.
Future programming may include other NASA+ original content, in-person live streaming events of NASA’s Artemis missions, including the first crewed mission to the Moon under the Artemis program, additional Europa content, and more. NASA+ also will remain available for free, with no ads, through the NASA app and on the agency’swebsite.
Earlier this year during itsIgnitionevent, NASA outlined a bold path forward for the agency, including increasing the cadence ofArtemismissions to the lunar surface, and building the firstMoon Base, among other agency priorities. Partnerships like this one help NASA maximize engagement with communities around the world by making the agency’s missions and educational content available to viewers on their preferred devices and channels.

item.title: Teams Lock in Mission Architecture for NASA’s SR-1 Freedom
item.description:
NASA completed a major review forSpace Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedomand locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time.
Experts from across the agency, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), and industry met at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland for a major SR-1 mission design review in October. Several key decisions were made, propelling the mission from an early concept toward a defined spacecraft design.
“SR-1 marks a pivotal step in how we travel through the solar system,” said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director. “This mission will be the first freight run on the railroad of the solar system, and the decisions we’re making now are laying the tracks for every nuclear-powered spacecraft that follows.”
Planned for launch in late 2028, SR-1 will use both nuclear and solar power to deliverSkyFall, a capsule carrying three next-generation helicopters, to Mars. Once deployed, the helicopters will study Martian geology and climate history, explore new terrain, and search for signs of subsurface ice.
As NASA prepares for more ambitious exploration missions, future spacecraft and surface operations will require significantly more power than current systems can provide, particularly in environments where sunlight is limited or unavailable. SR-1 will demonstrate how fission power can enable long-duration missions, pave the way for reliable surface power systems to support NASA’s futureMoon Base, and enable exploration deeper into the solar system.
The SR-1 Freedom spacecraft design has evolved since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman first introduced the concept in March at the agency’sIgnitionevent, where leadership shared plans to develop a fission-powered spacecraft in time for the next Mars launch window.
One significant change is to use a shorter boom than the one shown in early illustrations. The boom separates the reactor from the spacecraft’s main body, known as the Power and Propulsion Element. The shorter boom will reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design.
NASA and DOE experts also determined that improvements in shielding and spacecraft design will allow the reactor to operate closer to the rest of the spacecraft. This will simplify integration while maintaining the radiation protection needed for spacecraft electronics and the SkyFall payload.
Teams are continuing to evaluate other key design features, including the number of radiator panels on SR-1, output power levels of itsnuclear power module, and how long its reactor will operate. These decisions will help shape the final spacecraft design and ensure it meets mission objectives.
In addition, the team is modifying the spacecraft’sPower and Propulsion Elementby updating its communications system for the journey to Mars. SR-1 Freedom will use larger X-band antenna dishes to send data across deep space back to Earth. Further maturation of the spacecraft plans will focus on reducing risk, simplifying the design, and staying on schedule.
NASA awarded a $39.3 million contract to Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory to develop the heat rejection system for the spacecraft’s nuclear power module. The system will remove excess heat generated by the spacecraft’s nuclear power system, allowing it to operate safely and efficiently. The lab is working with the company Advanced Cooling Technologies as a key strategic commercial partner for providing the critical heat pipe and composite radiator technologies that will enable the system to meet the demanding mission requirements.
Awarded under the Aerospace Research, Development, and Engineering Support II contract, the contract action ensures the Applied Physics Laboratory team will design, build, test, and evaluate the system, along with producing the hardware needed for flight. The heat rejection system is a key part of demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in space and will help lay the groundwork and industrial production foundation for future high-power nuclear systems used in deep space exploration.
Along with the spacecraft design, teams have defined the mission timeline and planned operations.
After launch and once the spacecraft has left Earth orbit, SR-1 Freedom will activate and gradually increase reactor power. The reactor system will operate for an initial period of time before shutting down. During this period, the spacecraft will collect and send performance data back to Earth. Solar arrays will then provide power as it cruises to Mars.
After delivering SkyFall to Martian orbit, SR-1 Freedom will restart its fission reactor, collecting additional data on the spacecraft’s performance in deep space.

item.title: Amateur Astronomer? Be a Kilonova Catcher!
item.description:
Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called akilonova. These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory can watch the whole sky. But if you have a telescope with a camera, or access to one, you can help find and follow these cosmic fireworks as a part of NASA’sKilonova Catcherproject!
Kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network. Whengravitational wavedetectors or space telescopes send out an alert, volunteers point their own telescopes at the sky to help find and track the fading light. The network also follows up on gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the universe, and catches other short-lived cosmic events whenever the opportunity arises.
The Kilonova Catcher network has more than 150 registered members on several continents. Volunteers work side by side with professional astronomers and observatories. They have already contributed to more than 64 official reports shared through NASA’s General Coordinates Network, the system scientists use to share discoveries in real time. Volunteers’ observations have been credited for their contributions by being named authors in peer-reviewed scientific research papers. Kilonova Catcher volunteers also joined NASA’s lunarImpact Flash!project campaign during the Artemis II mission, recording the tiny flashes of light made when meteoroids strike the Moon. The network is getting ready to help follow up thousands of new alerts from NASA’s newNancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
"Here at Kilonova Catcher, by chasing the light from gravitational-wave events, we’re seeing how a single collision reaches across the universe,” said Cristina Andrade, Kilonova Catcher head of operations at the Minnesota Institute for Astrophysics. “The observatories that make this possible will produce an unprecedented amount of data. We need more human minds, more people with their eyes on the sky and on the data, both literally and figuratively. And more importantly, we need more people to realize they are capable of great feats of science, regardless of their background."
The Kilonova Catcher project is co-led by Andrade and Principal Investigator Dr. Damien Turpin, a researcher at the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA). Damien said, “I am inspired by the expertise and drive of our amateur astronomers. They are always digging for more information and pushing the limits of their understanding. This science could not be done without their contributions.”
To register and become a Kilonova Catcher, visithttps://kilonovacatcher.in2p3.fr/or send an email tokilonovacatcher@gmail.com. Anyone who has access to a telescope with a camera can take part!
Use your backyard telescope to spot the most cataclysmic collisions in our Universe!

item.title: NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Mission Overview
item.description:
NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the company’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft.
The Cygnus XL will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Following arrival to the station, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 to grapple the spacecraft before ground controllers robotically install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading.
In addition to food, supplies, and equipment for the crew, Cygnus will deliver several new experiments aimed at improving drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis treatment, predicting cancer spread, advancing treatments for muscle loss, improving radiation sensing, and supporting food production for future long-duration missions. This research includes:
Cardinal Muscle 2.0uses the microgravity environment to explore potential treatments for muscle loss. Muscle atrophy and strength loss experienced by astronauts after spaceflight share many features with age-related muscle decline on Earth and occur more rapidly in microgravity without exercise. Researchers will use a muscle tissue model to test different Food and Drug Administration-approved drugs used to treat other conditions can be repurposed to prevent or reduce muscle loss.
TheDNA Nano Binvestigation uses microgravity to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles designed to deliver medicine into dense tissues, such as cartilage and solid tumors. Microgravity may enable more uniform particle assembly, helping researchers refine production methods. The results could advance targeted treatments for cancer and osteoarthritis on Earth.
The Active Radiation Environment Sensor (ARES) will test a small radiation monitoring device to support future Artemis program and lunar missions. The system is designed to integrate with spacecraft systems and provide real-time radiation monitoring inside crew living areas. The results could inform radiation monitoring strategies and crew safety measures for future exploration missions.
Encapsulate-1uses miniature replicas of patients’ tumors to study how cancer cells move, invade surrounding tissues, and potentially spread. Researchers aim to develop a space-based diagnostic tool that could predict cancer progression months or even years in advance, improving early detection and treatment decisions for patients on Earth.
Ohalo IIIis a new plant growth facility designed to help food crop production on future long-duration missions. The mostly automated system uses innovative water recovery and air exchange technologies to grow a variety of crops. This research could help lead to better food production methods to keep crew healthy and fed on future exploration missions, including those to Mars.
JOining demonstrations IN-Space (JOINS)will mature technologies that allow robotic systems to join materials directly in space. In-space joining could enable large structures to be assembled and integrated after launch rather than being constrained by the size and volume of a launch vehicle. These capabilities may be needed to build and repair large infrastructure, such as structures that will to support future exploration underMoon Base.
Testing technologies in space helps validate their performance in unique environmental conditions, matures their readiness for operational use, reduces technical risk, and builds confidence for future mission applications.

item.title: Webb Reveals New Details in Supernova Remnant
item.description:
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the hot dust that makes up Cassiopeia A (Cas A) in this high-resolution, mid-infrared image released on Nov. 23, 2026. Remnants like these are the clouds of gas and dust that remain following the explosion of a massive star and will eventually seed a new generation of stars and planets. The Webb data supports a scenario in which the interior of the star underwent a dramatic change, possibly just hours before its demise.
See what scientists have learned about Cas A from Webb’s observation.
Image credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia University), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)

item.title: NASA’s Titan-Bound Dragonfly Rotorcraft Gets Its Eyes
item.description:
Science instruments for NASA’s Dragonfly are starting to arrive at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, where the car-sized rotorcraft is coming together for its mission to explore Saturn’s largest moon, Titan.
First to check in: DragonCam, which consists of seven cameras designed to characterizeTitan’s surface at multiple scales during flight and while on the ground. By mid-November, all seven cameras developed and built by Malin Space Science Systems had been installed in their insulated housings, tested, and integrated into the rotorcraft. Each camera will look out at Titan through a window in a foam enclosure that insulates the cameras and Dragonfly’s interior from Titan’s cryogenic environment, where ambient temperatures reach minus 290 degrees Fahrenheit.
A configurable LED array, built at APL and spanning the light spectrum from the infrared to the ultraviolet, provides information about the color of surface materials at the sampling site and helps scientists make inferences about their composition. During Titan’s long night, which spans nearly eight Earth days, these observations also may allow DragonCam to identify organic molecules that fluoresce under ultraviolet light. The LED illumination also allows us to see Titan as human eyes would.
“One of the most exciting things about Dragonfly is that we'll be able to see Titan from perspectives we've never had before,” said Elizabeth Turtle, Dragonfly principal investigator at APL. “With the capability to take images when Dragonfly is on the surface as well as while flying, DragonCam will give us both detailed views and sweeping panoramas of Titan's landscape, as well as insight into the processes that shaped this extraordinary world. Seeing these cameras become part of the Dragonfly lander is an exciting milestone that brings us another step closer to this unprecedented exploration.”
In addition to these science cameras, Dragonfly has two navigation cameras, also built by Malin Space Science Systems, that were installed this summer.
“We are extremely pleased to have delivered the DragonCam cameras,” said Michael Ravine, DragonCam development manager and a Dragonfly co-investigator from Malin Space Science Systems. “Now to have them on the Dragonfly spacecraft, taking images, it’s so much easier to picture how they will work on Titan. These will be our eyes to see and explore this whole new world.”
Two forward-mounted cameras — a wide-angle camera (WAC) and medium-angle camera (MAC) — are designed to capture images of the terrain in front of Dragonfly. The forward WAC offers a 90-degree field of view, while the forward MAC overlaps with the WAC, capturing part of that field of view at a higher resolution. Combined, the images from these two cameras provide a stereoscopic perspective from the front of the lander. Together with two additional side-mounted WACs, the system is able to capture panoramic views of the Titan landscape.
Two downward-facing WACs provide views of the surface beneath Dragonfly, helping the mission team decide if a landing spot is safe for deploying Dragonfly’s sample-collecting tool, known as DrACO, or Drill for Acquisition of Complex Organics, and its seismometer. A high-resolution microscopic imager will aim at DrACO’s drill site to pick out the details in millimeter-sized sand grains around the sampling location.
“DragonCam will give us critical context for the samples collected by DrACO,” said Carolyn Ernst, the DragonCam instrument scientist at APL. “We’ll be collecting materials at multiple sites across Titan, and the images from the cameras will help us relate the samples to Titan’s broader landscape and piece together the story of its geology.”
Components of Dragonfly's otherinstrument packages, DraGNS (Gamma-ray and Neutron Spectrometer), DraGMet (Geophysics and Meteorology), DraMS (Mass Spectrometer) and DrACO, are set for delivery, integration and testing over the next several months. Dragonfly is scheduled to launch in July 2028 and reach Titan in late 2034.

item.title: NASA Hubble’s New View of NGC 4394 Raises the Bar
item.description:
A brilliant galaxy with a distinct galactic bar takes center stage in this NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image. The galaxy, called NGC 4394, is in the constellation Coma Berenices (Berenice's Hair). At about 55 million light-years away, NGC 4394 is considered relatively nearby for a galaxy. It’s one of more than 1,000 galaxies that make up the Virgo Cluster, which is the galaxy cluster closest to us.
With its graceful spiral arms and central bar of stars, NGC 4394 closely resembles what astronomers think our home galaxy, the Milky Way, would look like if we were able to view it from a similar face-on vantage point. In a universe full of arcing spiral galaxies and nebulae organically shaped by the death and birth of stars, straight streaks of stars like NGC 4394’s galactic bar stand out. Galactic bars are extremely common; astronomers estimate 65 percent of nearby spiral galaxies have one. Hubble has imaged a wide variety of stunning barred spiral galaxies, includingNGC 5728,NGC 685, andNGC 613, but how do these striking features form?
Explanations for how galactic bars might form tend to center on a galaxy’s disk of stars becoming unstable. This could happen because of gravitational nudges from passing galaxies, interactions between stars, or other forces. Once the disk becomes unstable, the circular orbits of stars become elongated, leading to the barred shape seen in galaxies like NGC 4394. Observations show that galactic bars are more common among galaxies in the universe today than they were several billion years ago. Though stellar bars are in fashion today, research suggests that this is only temporary; as bars become more massive, they can themselves become unstable.
In addition to their stellar bars and spiral arms, NGC 4394 and the Milky Way galaxy share another important similarity, in that they might both contain a LINER (low-ionization nuclear emission-line region). LINER refers to an area near the center of a galaxy where its spectra feature certain ionized or neutral elements. Researchers do not yet know exactly how LINERs form, though either hungry supermassive black holes or intense star formation likely play a role.
Hubble has paid a visit to NGC 4394’s patch of sky more than once, and aprevious image of NGC 4394was released a decade ago. That image was part of an observing program (#10515; PI: Peng) that focused on NGC 4394’s galactic neighbor,Messier 85. While one of Hubble’s instruments examined Messier 85 to study its unusual collection of star clusters, another (Hubble'sAdvanced Camera for Surveys) captured a parallel area of the sky that contained NGC 4394.
Today’s image also incorporates observations from a recent program (#18103; PI: Thilker) dedicated to understanding how star formation comes to an end in galaxies in dense cluster environments, and how this process differs from more isolated galaxies adrift in the field. For this observing program, researchers used Hubble’sWide Field Camera 3and its sensitivity to a broad wavelength range to determine the ages of individual star clusters. NGC 4394 is one of 40 galaxies they studied in this way.
Claire AndreoliNASA'sGoddard Space Flight Center,Greenbelt, MDclaire.andreoli@nasa.gov

item.title: Eruption Extends Iwo Jima’s Beach
item.description:
A volcanic eruption just off the southeast shore of the Pacific island has reshaped the coast, but it’s unclear how long the new land will survive.
A volcanic eruption in the shallows near Iwo Jima has extended the Japanese island’s famed black sand beaches, at least temporarily.
Signs of unrest began in late October 2026. On October 27, seismic sensors recorded a sharp uptick in activity, and Japan’s Meteorological Agencyreportedthat the first photographs of the eruption were captured. Soon after, sensors on several satellites began to capture an array of observations.
TheOLI(Operational Land Imager) onLandsat 9captured the left image on October 26, when the coast was still quiet. On November 11, Landsat 9 got its first clear view of the land the submarine volcano has built (right). Ashortwave-infraredsignature, a sign of the eruption’s heat, is shown in orange. A faint gray volcanic plume drifts southeast of the vent, and a streak of floatingpumicestretches across the water in the same direction.
A false-color backscatter radar image from theNISAR(NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellite offered an even earlier look at the eruption. On October 28, despite heavy cloud cover, the radar detected alarge disturbancein the water in the same area that erupted in December 2023. When the clouds cleared in early November, theMODIS(Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) andVIIRS(Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) sensors on NASA and NOAA satellites also captured signs of the ongoing eruption’svolcanic plumes and infrared signature.
Japan’s Coast Guard released a report on November 16confirmingthe formation of new land connected to the pre-existing beach. The eruption appears to have added roughly 50 hectares (125 acres) of new beach, about the area of 90 American football fields. That would enlarge the island by about 1.7 percent. The new land adjoins the southeast beach where American troops landed on February 19, 1945, beginning one of thebloodiest battlesin the history of the U.S. Marines.
The location of the eruption is no surprise to scientists. In addition to the 2023 eruption off the southeast coast, Iwo Jima had an eruption off its west coast in August 2025, said Daniel Slayback, a scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center.
How long the new land will persist remains an open question. New land created by the 2023 eruption succumbed to wave action after just a few weeks, Slayback said. New land on volcanic islands has persisted more than a decade only a handful of times in recent times, including at Capelinhos, Surtsey, McDonald Island, and Home Reef, he added. “I imagine we’ll see this new land wash away within a few months,” he said. “But we’ll have to wait and see.”
Among the scientists watching closely is James Garvin, the chief scientist at Goddard and a geologist with a long-standing interest in how underwater volcanic eruptions create new islands and other landforms.
Typically,tephra-dominated eruptions like this form new land that is quickly “attacked” by ocean waves and other hydrologic forces, Garvin explained. An exception is when the eruption also injects certain types of lava that “cement” the ash into stronger material. “If we do see injection of basaltic-andesitic lava within the new materials, then it’s possible the new land could follow a pattern different from what we monitored in 2023,” he said.
NISAR will be especially valuable for tracking the site, Garvin said, because it makes frequent, high-resolutioninterferometricobservations through clouds and can show whether the new land erodes, subsides, or grows. The satellite has already recorded major changes at the eruption site betweenOctober 28 and November 11.
NASA scientists will also analyze sub-meter-resolution imagery from commercial satellites through NASA’sCommercial Satellite Data Acquisition Program. These images can reveal subtle deformation features like rilles, fractures, and cracks that offer clues about the stability of the new land.
Both Slayback and Garvin have studied new volcanic land before. They were part of a team that monitorednew landin the Kingdom of Tonga after an eruption in the Southwest Pacific but before most of it was obliterated during the highly explosiveHunga Tonga-Hunga Ha‘apai caldera collapse and eruptionin January 2022.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from theU.S. Geological Survey.Story by Adam Voiland.
